nameStory: Berkeley's polypore honors Miles Joseph Berkeley, a pioneering English mycologist who studied fungi in the 1800s. The delightful alternate name 'stump blossoms' comes from the way these large, fan-shaped fungi bloom like enormous flowers from the bases of oak trees and stumps.
description: Berkeley's polypore is one of New England's most impressive bracket fungi, forming massive rosettes that can span several feet across. These shelf-like fungi grow in overlapping, fan-shaped brackets with creamy white to yellowish caps when young, becoming brownish with age. The undersides have tiny pores instead of gills, and the whole fruiting body has a thick, meaty texture. This parasitic fungus attacks the roots and lower trunks of oak and other hardwood trees, eventually causing them to weaken and fall.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Undersides have tiny white pores that bruise brown when pressed - run your finger across them to see this color change reaction

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Multiple overlapping fan-shaped brackets form rosette clusters, cream-colored when fresh, aging to tan or brown with a velvety texture

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, stubby central stem or multiple stems merge together at the base, often partially buried in soil and leaf litter

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, slightly fruity or yeasty aroma, becoming more earthy as they age

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Young caps feel firm and meaty like a thick steak, becoming tougher and more leathery with age - they're surprisingly heavy when fresh

habitat: Look for Berkeley's polypore at the bases of oak trees and other hardwoods throughout New England's forests, particularly in mature deciduous and mixed woodlands. They typically grow directly from roots, trunk bases, or nearby stumps in rich, moist soils. You'll often find them in the same spots year after year, as the fungus continues attacking the same root systems.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins in late spring, appearing as small white knobs at the base of infected trees that are easily overlooked.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season produces the most impressive specimens - large, fresh rosettes with bright white pore surfaces and firm, meaty texture perfect for identification.
seasonality.fall: Mature fruiting bodies become tougher and more brownish, but are still easily spotted and identified by their distinctive rosette shape and bruising pores.
seasonality.winter: Old, weathered specimens persist on trees as dark, woody brackets that help you locate spots to watch for fresh growth next year.

funFact: A single Berkeley's polypore can weigh over 50 pounds when fresh and continue growing from the same root system for many years - some specimens have been documented returning to the exact same spot for over a decade, getting larger each time!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with hen-of-the-woods (maitake), but Berkeley's polypore has pores that bruise brown when touched, while hen-of-the-woods has pores that don't change color. Remember: 'Berkeley bruises brown' - if pressing the pores doesn't cause browning, it's probably maitake.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a polypore (pore fungus), Berkeley's polypore was recently moved from the traditional polypore family into the Russulaceae family, which includes milk caps and brittlegills - this reflects new DNA research showing its true evolutionary relationships.
compareHints: Berkeley's polypore is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our bracket fungi. Within the broader Russulaceae family, it's completely different from its relatives like milk caps and brittlegills, which have gills and grow from soil rather than forming woody brackets on trees. No other New England polypore forms such large, meaty rosettes with brown-bruising pores.
